case_name: Parmar v. Blenz The Canadian Coffee Company Ltd.
text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF
BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Parmar v. Blenz The Canadian Coffee Company Ltd.,

2007 BCSC 1190

Date: 20070807

Docket: S041926

Registry:
Vancouver

Between:

Jaspal Parmar, Mya Enterprises Corporation, Elme
Wadi,

Wadi Coffee Limited dba Blenz Coffee, Peggy Lemaire,

Xavier Lemaire, and Mekvent Enterprises Limited

Plaintiffs

And

Blenz The Canadian Coffee Company Ltd. and KAD Coffee
Co. Ltd.,

Blenz Coffee Ltd., Michael Golden, Michael Golden Law Corporation

Defendants

Before: The Honourable Mr. Justice Chamberlist

Reasons for Judgment

In Chambers

Counsel for the plaintiffs (respondents) Jaspal Parmar and
Mya Enterprises Corporation:

G. Hagel

Counsel for defendants (applicants) Blenz The Canadian
Coffee Company Ltd. and Blenz Coffee Ltd.:

J.D. Shields

Date and Place of Hearing:

March 15, 2007

Vancouver, B.C.

[
1
]

The applicant defendants have filed its notice of motion dated December
14, 2006, seeking the following relief:

1.         The plaintiffs post security for costs in the
amount of $53,595.15;

2.         Striking
all or portions of the amended statement of claim as it refers to Mya
Enterprises Ltd.;

3.         Striking
all or portions of the amended statement of claim as it refers to Mekvent
Enterprises Limited;

4.         Dismissing
all or portions of the claim by the plaintiffs Jaspal Parmar and Mya
Enterprises Corporation; and

5.         Costs.

[
2
]

The applicant relies on Supreme Court Rules 1(5), 31(6), 19(24)(a)
through (d), and 57 and the inherent jurisdiction of the court and
s. 236
of
the
Business Corporations Act
, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57.

[
3
]

The defendant, KAD Coffee Co. Ltd. (“KAD”) supports the relief sought by
the applicant/defendant.

[
4
]

The application for security of costs is only with respect to the
corporate entity, Mya Enterprises Corporations (“Mya”) and no submissions were
made by the applicant with respect to its motion seeking an order striking all
or portions of the amended statement of claim as it refers to Mekvent
Enterprises Limited (“Mekvent”).

[
5
]

The relevant provisions of the Rules of Court relied upon by the
applicant are as follows:

19(7)     A party
shall not plead an allegation of fact or a new ground or claim inconsistent
with the party’s previous pleading.

19(24)   At any
stage of a proceeding the court may order to be struck out or amended the whole
or any part of an endorsement, pleading, petition or other document on the
ground that

(a)        it
discloses no reasonable claim or defence as the case may be,

(b)        it is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous
or vexatious,

(c)        it
may prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial or hearing or the proceeding,
or

(d)        it
is otherwise an abuse of the process of the court,

and the court may grant judgment or order the proceeding to be
stayed or dismissed and may order the costs of the application to be paid as
special costs.

31(6)     An
application for judgment or any other application may be made to the court
using as evidence

(a)        admissions
of the truth of a fact or the authenticity of a document made

(i)         in
an affidavit or pleading filed by a party,

(ii)         in
an examination for discovery of a party or a person examined for discovery on
behalf of a party, or

(iii)        in
response to a notice to admit, or

(b)        admissions
of the truth of a fact or the authenticity of a document deemed to be made
under subrule (2)

and the court may, without waiting for the determination of
any other question between the parties, make any order it thinks just.

And the relevant provision of the
Business
Corporations Act
is:

236       If a corporation is the
plaintiff in a legal proceeding brought before the court, and if it appears
that the corporation will be unable to pay the costs of the defendant if the
defendant is successful in the defence, the court may require security to be
given by the corporation for those costs, and may stay all legal proceedings until
the security is given.

[
6
]

The costs sought to be paid by the defendant Mya is $53,595.15 based on
Scale B, assuming a ten day trial.

[
7
]

The action itself contains allegations by the plaintiffs with respect to
two franchise agreements, but this application of the applicant/defendants
dealt solely with the franchise agreement concerning Jaspal Parmar and Mya.
The action against Michael Golden and Michael Golden Law Corporation deals with
allegations of breach of an agreement for legal services provided to the plaintiffs
Mya and Parmar by Michael Golden and Michael Golden Law Corporation.

BACKGROUND

[
8
]

In or about 2001 Jaspal Parmar entered into an agreement with the
defendant Blenz The Canadian Coffee Company Ltd. (“Blenz”) for the acquisition
of a Blenz franchise in Coquitlam, B.C.   Mr. Parmar, in his amended statement
of claim, says that he and the defendant Blenz entered into a franchise
agreement and entered into a sublease with Blenz Coffee Ltd. (“the Blenz
sub-landlord”).  The franchise agreement was executed on or about September 17,
2001 (“the Parmar agreement”).  At para. 19 of the amended statement of claim,
this allegation appears:

The Parmar agreement was the result
of negotiations conducted in the latter half of 2001 between Parmar in his
personal capacity and as the anticipated owner, director, officer and agent of
Mya Enterprises a representative of Blenz.  At all material times, to the
knowledge of Blenz, Parmar intended to assign the Parmar agreement to a company
to be incorporated for the purpose of operating the Coquitlam franchise, namely
Mya Enterprises.  By assignment agreement dated September 17, 2001 Blenz,
Parmar and Mya Enterprises entered into a written assignment agreement pursuant
to which Parmar assigned the Parmar agreement to Mya Enterprises.

[
9
]

A representative of the defendants Blenz The Canadian Coffee Company
Ltd. and Blenz Coffee Ltd. has deposed that notwithstanding the fact that the
assignment was dated September 17, 2001 it was actually executed in April of
2002.  This would appear to be correct given that the plaintiff Mya was not
incorporated until October 11, 2001.

[
10
]

At para. 21 of the amended statement of claim, this assertion appears:

On or about October 11, 2001, Mya
Enterprises Corporation was incorporated pursuant to the laws of British
Columbia.  At all material times, with the knowledge and approval of Blenz, Mya
Enterprises was operating the Coquitlam franchise under the terms of the Parmar
agreement.

[
11
]

In addition, the applicants submit that the assertion found in paras. 22
to 24 of the amended statement of claim, that during the course of negotiations
leading up to the Parmar agreement Blenz made certain representations to Parmar
in his personal capacity and as a representative of Mya, should be struck out
on the basis that this is contrary to the evidence of Parmar himself when he
swore that he entered into the agreement.  The applicants point to Parmar
affidavit #1, and particularly paras. 2, 3, 4 and 5 thereof, where Parmar
himself swore that the alleged misrepresentations were made to him and that he
entered the franchise agreement.  Those paras. provide as follows:

2.         In
2001, Blenz provided me with a Pro Forma Document identifying projected
revenues, expenses and profits for a Blenz franchise to be opened at Coquitlam
Centre.  . . .

3.         In
2001, Blenz provided me with a Summary Report for the Coquitlam Blenz.  . . .

4.         In
2001, I entered into an agreement with Blenz for the acquisition of the
Coquitlam Blenz franchise.  . . .

5.         Prior to signing the
franchise agreement, I was advised that I would be required to pay $25,000 for
the Blenz franchise and an additional sum for the renovation of the Coquitlam
Blenz.  If the renovation cost less than the sum I paid I would receive that
money back.  If it cost more, I would pay the extra.

[
12
]

The applicants submit that as Mya Enterprises was not even incorporated
until October 11, 2001, there could not have been anything that happened
relative to Mya because Mya was not incorporated.

[
13
]

As a result, the applicants submit that Mya could have no possible claim
against Blenz for any acts alleged prior to its legal creation and, as such,
paras. 4, 19 to 31 inclusive, and the balance of the amended statement of claim
as it refers to Mya prior to its legal creation should be struck.  Paragraphs
4, 19 to 31 provide as follows:

4.         Mya Enterprises carried on business through a Blenz
The Canadian Coffee Company (“Blenz”) franchise at Unit 1206, Coquitlam Centre,
2929 Barnet Highway, Coquitlam, British Columbia (the “Coquitlam Store”).

. . .

19.        The Parmar Agreement was the result of negotiations
conducted in the later half of 2001 between Parmar, in his personal capacity
and as the anticipated owner, director, officer and agent of Mya Enterprises
and representatives of Blenz.  At all material times, to the knowledge of
Blenz, Parmar intended to assign the Parmar Agreement to a company to be
incorporated for the purpose of operating the Coquitlam Franchise, namely Mya
Enterprises.

20.        On or about September 17, 2001, Blenz, Parmar, and
Mya Enterprises entered into a written Assignment Agreement pursuant to which
Parmar assigned the Parmar Agreement to Mya Enterprises.

21.        On or about October 11, 2001, Mya Enterprises
Corporation was incorporated pursuant to the laws of British Columbia.  At all
material times, with the knowledge and approval of Blenz, Mya Enterprises was
operating the Coquitlam Franchise under the terms of the Parmar Agreement.

Negligent Misrepresentation and Breach of Duty of Good Faith

22.        During the course of the negotiations leading up to
the Parmar Agreement, Blenz represented to Parmar in his personal capacity and
as a representative of Mya Enterprises that:

(a)        the
annual sales, gross profits, and operating costs for the Coquitlam Franchise
for its first three years of operation would be as follows (the “Parmar
Estimates”):

Year One

Year Two

Year Three

Projected Sales

$655,000

$800,00

$880,000

Cost of Goods Sold

33%

216,150

264,000

290,400

Gross Profit

$438,850

$536,000

$589,600

Operating Costs:

Occupancy Cost

86,600

112,250

120,100

Wages

20%

131,000

160,000

176,000

Royalties

8%

52,500

64,000

70,400

Advertising

2%

13,100

16,000

17,600

Misc.

3%

19,650

24,000

26,400

Total Operating Costs:

$302,750

$376,250

$410,500

NET OPERATING PROFIT

Net operating profit before
Taxes, Depreciation, Debt Service and Owners Salary

$136,100

$159,750

$179,100

(b)        the
Parmar Estimates were based on the actual performance and financial statements
of similar operations;

(c)        the
Parmar Estimates were created using reasonable assumptions; and

(d)        the
occupancy costs for the Coquitlam Franchise would be as follows (the “Occupancy
Costs”):

Year 1:

$8275/month plus GST

Year 2:

$8375/month plus GST

Year 3:

$8875/month plus GST

Year 4:

$8975/month plus GST

Year 5:

$9075/month plus GST

Year 6:

$9875/month plus GST

Year 7:

$9975/month plus GST

Year 8:

$10,775/month plus GST

Year 9:

$10,900/month plus GST

Year 10:

$11,000/month plus GST; and

(e)        the
Occupancy Costs included all occupancy-related expenses, including hydro and
property taxes.

(collectively the “Parmar Representations”)

23.        Particulars of the Parmar Representations are as
follows:

(a)        the
Parmar Representations were contained in a document entitled “Blenz Coffee,
Coquitlam Centre Mall, Proforma” and in a document entitled “Summary Report”,
both provided by Blenz to Parmar in or about September 2001; and

(b)        the
Parmar Representations were repeated and referred to by representatives of
Blenz, including Mark West, then Blenz’s Manager of Franchises and now its Vice
President Operations (“West”), on multiple occasions during the course of
negotiations held in September 2001 between Blenz and Parmar leading up to the
execution of the Parmar Agreement.

24.        Blenz intended and knew, or alternatively ought to
have known, that Parmar in his personal capacity and as the anticipated owner,
director, officer and agent for Mya Enterprises would rely on the Parmar
Representations and be induced by them to:

(a)        enter in the Parmar Agreement with Blenz;

(b)        purchase and operate the Coquitlam
Franchise;

(c)        pay
the amount of $225,990 (plus taxes) to Blenz in respect of the Parmar Agreement
and the Coquitlam Franchise (the “Parmar Payment”);

(d)        invest
additional funds in the Coquitlam Franchise in the course of operating the Coquitlam
Franchise;

(e)        assign
(in the case of Parmar) and accept the assignment of (in the case of Mya
Enterprises) the Parmar Agreement and the Coquitlam Franchise; and

(f)         enter
into a Sublease with the Blenz Sub Landlord.

25.        Parmar and Mya Enterprises reasonably relied on the
Parmar Representations and were induced by the Parmar Representations to do the
acts set out in paragraph 24 above.

26.        Blenz was negligent in making the Parmar
Representations which were false and misleading in that:

(a)        the
actual sales, gross profit, and net operating profit for the Coquitlam
Franchise were much lower than projected;

(b)        the
cost of goods and the operating costs for the Coquitlam Franchise were much
higher than projected;

(c)        there
were no comparable franchises in operation at the time of the negotiations
leading up to the Parmar Agreement;

(d)        few,
if any, franchises have ever obtained the sales or profits projected in the
Parmar estimates;

(e)        the
Parmar Estimates were not based on the actual performance and financial
statements of similar operations;

(f)         the
Parmar Estimates were not created using reasonable assumptions;

(g)        at
the time of the Parmar Representations, Blenz knew that the actual occupancy
costs for Year 2 would be $9,333/month plus GST, plus hydro-electric costs and
property taxes;

(h)        as Blenz
knew at the time of the Parmar Representations, the Occupancy Costs did not in
fact include hydro-electric costs and property taxes.  Blenz subsequently
billed these charges to Mya Enterprises in addition to the monthly Occupancy
Costs;

(i)         as
Blenz knew that few, if any, franchisees had ever obtained the sales or profits
projected in the Parmar Estimates; and

(j)         as
Blenz knew that no comparable franchisees had ever obtained the sales or
profits projected in the Parmar Estimates.

26.1      Parmar
and Mya further say that Blenz had a duty of good faith when it prepared the
Parmar Estimates and provided the Parmar Estimates to Parmar.

26.2      Parmar
and Mya say that Blenz breached its duty of good faith when Blenz prepared the
Parmar Estimates and provided the Parmar Estimates to Parmar as:

(a)        Blenz
knew that few, if any, franchisees had ever obtained the sales or profits
projected in the Parmar Estimates;

(b)        Blenz
did not warn Parmar and Mya that few, if any, franchisees had ever obtained the
sales or profits projected in the Parmar Estimates;

(c)        Blenz
knew that no comparable franchisees ever obtained the sales or profits
projected in the Parmar Estimates;

(d)        Blenz
did not warn Parmar and Mya that no comparable franchisees ever obtained the
sales or profits projected in the Parmar Estimates.

27.        As a
consequence of the negligent misrepresentations made by Blenz as set out above
and Blenz’s breach of its duty of good faith to Parmar and Mya, Parmar and Mya
are entitled to rescission of the Parmar Agreement.

28.        As a
further consequence of the negligent misrepresentations made by Blenz as set
out above and Blenz’s breach of its duty of good faith to Parmar and Mya, the
consideration for the Parmar Payment has wholly failed and Blenz has had and
received the said Parmar Payment to the use of Parmar and Mya Enterprises, who
became and are entitled to be repaid the Parmar Payment.

Beach of
Collateral Agreement

29.        On or
about September 17, 2001, Blenz, Mya Enterprises, and Parmar entered into a
collateral agreement relating to Parmar’s acquisition of the Coquitlam
Franchise (the “Parmar Collateral Agreement”).  The terms of the Parmar
Collateral Agreement included:

(a)        Blenz
represented and warranted that the Parmar Representations were true and
accurate; and

(b)        in
return, Parmar agreed to enter into the Parmar Agreement and Parmar and Mya
Enterprises agreed to enter into the Assignment Agreement and Parmar and Mya
agreed to enter into a sublease with a company affiliated with Blenz.

30.        As a
result of the Parmar Representations being false and misleading as set out
above, Blenz breached the Parmar Collateral Agreement.  As a result of this
breach, the consideration for Parmar to enter into the Parmar Agreement and for
Parmar and Mya Enterprises to enter into the Assignment Agreement and Mya and
Parmar to enter into the Sublease has wholly failed, and Parmar and Mya
Enterprises are entitled to rescission of these agreements.  Further, Blenz has
had and received the Parmar Payment to the use of Parmar and Mya Enterprises,
who became and are entitled to be repaid the Parmar Payment.

Damages

31.        Further, and in the
alternative, by reason of Blenz’s negligent misrepresentations and breach of
the Parmar Collateral Agreement, Blenz’s duties of good faith, Blenz’s breach
of Blenz’s duties as an agent, all as set out above, Parmar and Mya Enterprises
have suffered loss and damage, particulars of which include loss of the Parmar
Payment, loss of the further amounts invested by them during the operation of
the Coquitlam Franchise (including amounts contributed to the Advertising Fund,
as set out below), lost profits, loss of opportunity, and damage to their
business and reputation.

[
14
]

The applicants also submit that the evidence of Parmar are admissions
under R. 31(6) and that the claim respecting Mya should be struck or
alternatively the claims relating to Mya are contrary to R. 19(24)(a) through
(d).  Further, the applicants submit that paras. 23 and 24(f), as set out
above, is inconsistent with para. 16.3 of the amended statement of claim, which
provides:

16.3      Mya entered into an
agreement with the Blenz Sub Landlord for the sublease of the Coquitlam Store
(the “Sublease”).

[
15
]

The applicants submit that R. 19(7) bars pleading inconsistent allegations
and therefore such pleas are inconsistent with para. 16.3 and therefore should
be struck.

[
16
]

Further, the applicants say that the evidence with respect to who
entered into agreements comes from Mr. Parmar himself at para. 5 of his
affidavit #3 where he states:

After I entered into the franchise
agreement with the Defendant Blenz the Canadian Coffee Company Ltd., I entered
into a sublease for a Blenz coffee store from Blenz Coffee Ltd. (the “Sublease”).

[
17
]

The applicants submit that given the sworn evidence of Mr. Parmar, which
the applicants submit is an admission, the claims by Mya and Parmar in regard
to the sublease cannot be maintained and therefore paras. 16.3, 24, 29(b) and
30 of the amended statement of claim should be struck.

[
18
]

The applicants submit that these pleadings are inconsistent with the
admissions of Parmar and are also contrary to R. 19(24)(a) through (d) and
therefore ought to be struck.

[
19
]

Further the applicants submit that Mya cannot allege, as it has in
paras. 22 to 26 of the amended statement of claim, that Blenz made
representations to it prior to the Parmar agreement of September 17, 2001, and breached
an alleged duty of good faith prior to the Parmar agreement aforesaid in paras.
26.1 to 28 of the amended statement of claim because, with respect to these
allegations, the applicants again say that these allegations cannot possibly be
true in regard to Mya as it was not incorporated until October 11, 2001.

[
20
]

Lastly, in regard to the allegations of both Parmar and Mya, the applicants
say that even if Mya was incorporated, which it was not, the existence of an
entire agreement clause in the franchise agreement and the further clause that
the franchisee has made an independent investigation of the business and that
he has had an adequate opportunity to be advised by advisors of his own
choosing, cannot succeed because the terms of the franchise agreement and the
terms of the assignment agreement prohibit such a claim.  In support of this
assertion the applicants rely on cases which have dealt with the interpretation
of an entire agreement clause, including the following cases –
Sultani v.
Blenz the Canadian Coffee Company Ltd.
,
2005 BCCA 578
;
A-Wear
Clothing Incorporated v. Axiom Fashions Ltd.
,
2002 BCSC 316
;
Salem
v. Priority Building Services Ltd. et al
,
2004 BCSC 1324
; and
Salem
v. Priority Building Services
,
2005 BCCA 617
.

[
21
]

As such, the following relief is sought by the applicants:

1.         That
the corporate Plaintiffs Mya and Mekvent post security for costs, each in the
amount of $53,595.15 and that until they do, their claims are stayed.

2.         Paragraphs
16.3, 24, 29(b) and 30 of the Amended Statement of Claim should be struck with
regard to Mya.

3.         And
that paragraphs 18-31 and paragraphs 1(a), 1(c) and 1(d) of the Prayer for
Relief of the Amended Statement of Claim be struck.

4.         Costs, payable forthwith, in
any event, and assessed at $500 as against each Plaintiff.

DISCUSSION

[
22
]

I will first deal with the position taken by the applicants that various
pleadings are inconsistent with the admissions of Parmar and therefore ought to
be struck on the basis of them being inconsistent allegations under R. 19(7),
which provides:

(7)        A party shall not plead an
allegation of fact or a new ground or claim inconsistent with the party’s
previous pleading.

[
23
]

I do note that this Rule was not relied upon in the notice of motion,
however, argument was made with respect to it.

[
24
]

The affect of this subrule is primarily to prevent a party from setting
up a claim in a subsequent pleading which is inconsistent with an earlier
pleading.  It should be noted that the following subrule, being 19(8),
provides:

(8)        Subrule (7) does not affect
the right of a party to make allegations in the alternative or to amend or
apply for leave to amend a pleading.

[
25
]

In the recent decision of
Gabbs v. Bouwhuis
, [2005] B.C.J.
No. 2776,
2005 BCSC 1782
, Bennett J., at para. 23, approved the following
statement found in “The Law of Civil Procedure, Volume 2”:

The Rule simply means that a
party’s second pleading must not contradict the first.  A plaintiff must not
set up in his reply a new cause of action which is not raised in the statement
of claim.

[
26
]

In the same case, her Ladyship went on to consider both subrules and
concluded, at para. 24:

. . . A party may plead
inconsistent claims in the statement of claim and defence.  The party cannot,
however, make an alternative claim that is inconsistent in reply or in defence
to a counterclaim.

[
27
]

In the case at bar, it is clear from the amended statement of claim that
what is alleged is that at all material times Mr. Parmar made it known to the
representatives of Blenz that he was acting in his own personal capacity and as
the principal of Mya.  As a result, it is arguable on the pleadings that Blenz
and Blenz Coffee Ltd. are estopped from denying the existence of the agreement
and that Parmar was acting in a dual capacity as alleged.

[
28
]

Questions relating to what activities were done and by whom, and in what
capacity, are matters to be proven or disproved through discovery and or
trial.

[
29
]

Further Rule 19(7) prohibits inconsistent claims in subsequent pleadings
such as an inconsistency between a statement of claim and a reply to a
counterclaim and is therefore not a basis for striking portions of a statement
of claim under R. 19(7) or under R. 19(24).

[
30
]

I therefore turn to the applicants’ reliance on R. 19(24).

[
31
]

In
Isaac v. Guardian Capital Group et al
,
2004 BCSC 254
,
Mr. Justice Melnick succinctly reviewed and summarized the law on the
principals governing applications under R. 19(24) of the Rules of Court:

[7]

While the B.C. Defendants complain of a variety of breaches of Rule 19,
the remedy for those breaches is in Rule 19(24). That Rule reads as follows:

At any stage of a proceeding the
court may order to be struck out or amended the whole or any part of an
endorsement, pleading, petition or other document on the ground that

(a)        it
discloses no reasonable claim or defence as the case may
be,

(b)        it is
unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious,

(c)        it
may prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial or hearing or the proceeding,
or

(d)        it is
otherwise an abuse of the process of the court,

and the court may grant judgment or
order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and may order the costs of the
application to be paid as special costs.

[8]

In practice, a party attacking pleadings often makes reference to Rule
19(24) as a whole instead of relying on particular subrules.  The B.C.
Defendants in this case are guilty of such a broad-brush approach.
Consequently, courts often gloss over which part of the rule they are
applying in their analysis.  Thus, it is useful to review how each rule
has been interpreted in order to be able to rely on the appropriate aspect of
Rule 19(24).

[9]

Regardless of the subrule in 19(24) relied on, the B.C. Court of Appeal
in
Kripps v. Touche Ross & Co.
(1992),
1992 CanLII 923 (BC CA)
, 94 D.L.R. (4th) 284,
makes clear at 289 that the court must decide an application under Rule 19(24)
on the pleadings either as they stand or as they may be amended.

1. Rule 19(24)(a)

[10]

The standard on a Rule 19(24)(a) application is well established.
In
Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc.
,
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959, the
plaintiff suffered illness from exposure to asbestos in the course of his work
as an electrician.  He accused several companies in the asbestos
manufacturing and use business of conspiracy to hide the fact that asbestos
fibres could cause disease.  The defendant Carey brought an application
under Rule 19(24)(a) to have the conspiracy claim dismissed.  The Supreme
Court of Canada noted at paragraph 12 that Rule 19(24) is a codification of the
court’s inherent jurisdiction to stay actions that are an abuse of process or
that do not disclose a reasonable cause of action.  After considering
similar rules in England and in Ontario, as well as jurisprudence from B.C. and
the Supreme Court of Canada, the court set the following test at page 980:

… assuming that the facts as stated
in the statement of claim can be proved, is it “plain and obvious” that the
plaintiff’s statement of claim discloses no reasonable cause of action?
As in England, if there is a chance that the plaintiff might succeed,
then the plaintiff should not be “driven from the judgment seat”.  Neither
the length and complexity of the issues, the novelty of the cause of action,
nor the potential for the defendant to present a strong defence should prevent
the plaintiff from proceeding with his or her case.  Only if the action is
certain to fail because it contains a radical defect ranking with the others
listed in Rule 19(24) of the British Columbia
Rules of Court
should the
relevant portions of a plaintiff’s statement of claim be struck out under Rule
19(24)(a).

[11]

Any doubt about whether or not a plaintiff has satisfied the test set
out in
Hunt
is to be resolved in the plaintiff’s favour:
Citizens
for Foreign Aid Reform Inc.
v.
Canadian Jewish Congress

(1999),

1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, 36 C.P.C. (4th) 266 (B.C.S.C.).

2. Rule 19(24)(b)

[12]

The standard under Rule 19(24)(b) is also a “plain and obvious” one,
though it must be plain and obvious that the pleading is unnecessary,
scandalous, frivolous or vexatious. Mr. Justice Romilly in
Citizens for
Foreign Aid
sets out a useful summary of the jurisprudence on this
subrule and parts of subrule 19(24)(c) at paragraph 47:

Irrelevancy and embarrassment are
both established when pleadings are so confusing that it is difficult to
understand what is being pleaded:
Gittings v. Caneco Audio-Publishers Inc.

(1987),
1987 CanLII 2561 (BC SC)
, 17 B.C.L.R. (2d) 38 (B.C. S.C.)…. A pleading is "unnecessary"
or "vexatious" if it does not go to establishing the plaintiff's
cause of action or does not advance any claim known in law:
Strauts v.
Harrigan
(December 2, 1991), Doc. Vancouver C913631 (B.C. S.C.)…. A
pleading is "frivolous" if it is obviously unsustainable, not in the
sense that it lacks an evidentiary basis, but because of the doctrine of
estoppel:
Chrisgian v. B.C. Rail Ltd.
(July 3, 1992), Doc. Prince George
20714 (B.C. Master).

3. Rule 19(24)(c)

[13]

Mr. Justice Hutcheon in

Keddie v. Dumas Hotels Ltd.

(1985),
1985 CanLII 417 (BC CA)
, 62 B.C.L.R. 145 (C.A.), sets out succinctly at page 147 what
constitutes an embarrassing pleading within the meaning of Rule 19(24)(c),
citing
Mayor of City of London v. Herner
(1914), 111 L.T. 512
(C.A.) at 514:

… the allegations are so irrelevant
that to allow them to stand would involve useless expense, and would also
prejudice the trial of the action by involving the parties in a dispute that is
wholly apart from the issues.  In order that allegations should be
struck out from a defence upon that ground ... their irrelevancy must be quite
clear and, so to speak, apparent at the first glance.

4. Rule 19(24)(d)

[14]

This section is normally reserved for claims that clearly cannot stand
for such reasons as
res judicata
and issue estoppel:
World Wide Treasure
Adventures Inc. v. Trivia Games Inc.
(1996),
1996 CanLII 1428 (BC CA)
, 17 B.C.L.R. (3d) 187
(C.A.).  Notwithstanding the fact that the B.C. Defendants have not
excluded reliance on this subrule, I do not consider that such issues arise in
this case.

[
32
]

In a case decided later that year (
McNutt v. Canada (Attorney
General)
,
2004 BCSC 1113
) Allan J. said this at para. 42 with respect
to pleadings which are an abuse of process:

[42]

A pleading is an abuse of process if the litigation process is used for
an improper purpose; e.g. where the proceedings constitute a sham, where the
process of the court is not being fairly or honestly used, or is employed for
some ulterior or improper purpose:
Babavic v. Babowech,
[1993]
B.C.J. No. 1802 (S.C.) (QL)
; Drinking Driving Awareness Corp. v. British
Columbia
(5 December 2003), New Westminster Registry S78513.
In
Babavic,
the Court found that the plaintiffs’ action was
an abuse of the court’s process because it was a vexatious suit without merit
brought with the sole motive and intent to harass one of the defendants and
interfere with her ability to enforce a judgment.  In
Drinking
Driving Awareness Corp.
, the Court struck out the plaintiffs’ claims
against a number of defendants including Her Majesty the Queen, the Premier,
the Provincial and Federal Attorney Generals and a Crown counsel. The
plaintiffs did not attend the application, which was brought by some, but not
all, of the defendants.  Madam Justice Koenigsberg found the statement of
claim and particulars incomprehensible and incapable of amendment.
Invoking her inherent jurisdiction, she dismissed the action in its entirety,
even against the defendants who had not brought an application to strike.

[
33
]

With respect to an application under R. 19(24) the court must proceed on
the assumption that the facts pleaded are true (
Hunt v. Carey Canada,
Inc.
,
supra
), and for an applicant to succeed it must be plain
and obvious that the impugned pleadings offend the subrules in R. 19(24), and
the court must not weigh the evidence or closely examine the affidavits, and in
fact, must give the benefit of any doubt to the plaintiff.

[
34
]

I am of the opinion that the provisions said to be inconsistent do not
meet any of the criteria discussed by Mr. Justice Melnick in his review of R.
19(24) and under R. 19(24)(a) it is not plain and obvious that the provisions
disclose no reasonable cause of action.

[
35
]

Similarly, under subrule (b), I have concluded that the impugned
pleadings do not meet any of the criteria in that they are not obviously
unsustainable save and except for any pleading that alleges that Mya relied on
representations in the alleged collateral agreement or in the Parmar
agreement.  These allegations cannot be true because of the fact that Mya was
not incorporated until sometime later as evidenced by the plaintiff’s own
pleadings.  It may well come to pass that it will be found as a fact that the
individual plaintiff, Parmar, negotiated and signed in a dual capacity, but
that does not mean that the representations that were made in the collateral agreement
or the franchise agreement could be relied on by a party that was not legally
in existence at the material time.

[
36
]

With respect to those allegations I have concluded that it is
appropriate to strike out any references that allege representations were made
to Mya before its incorporation.  With that in mind I would strike out the
following portions of the amended statement of claim:

Para. 16.3

Mya entered into an
agreement with the Blenz Sub Landlord for the sublease of the Coquitlam Store
(the “Sublease”).

Para. 22

. . . in his personal
capacity and as a representative of Mya Enterprises . . .

Para. 24(f)

enter into a Sublease with
the Blenz Sub Landlord.

Para. 25

. . . and Mya Enterprises
reasonably . . .

Para. 26.1

. . . and Mya further . . .
[says]

Para. 26.2

. . . and Mya . . . [says]

Para. 27

. . . and Mya . . .

Para. 28

. . . and Mya . . .

Para 29

. . . Mya Enterprises, . .
.

Para. 29(b)

. . . and Mya Enterprises .
. . and Mya . . .

Para. 30

. . . and Mya and . . .

and amend para. 24(f) to restrict it to an allegation
only with respect to Parmar.

[
37
]

The applicants argued at length that certain aspects of the plaintiffs’
claim including the collateral agreement and the misrepresentation regarding
annual sales, gross profits and operating costs as set out in para. 22 of the
statement of claim, are doomed to fail because of case law respecting exclusion
clauses.  That, of course, is a matter for trial.  Notwithstanding that there
are very recent cases where the franchisor has been successful in defeating
this type of assertion, there are cases which have not been overruled by the
Court of Appeal where a franchisee has succeeded in the types of arguments
advanced by the plaintiffs here (
Zippy Print Enterprises Ltd. v. Pawliuk

(1994), 100 B.C.L.R. (2d) (C.A.)).

[
38
]

Given the existence of this type of case, I am unable to say that the
plaintiffs’ claim discloses no reasonable claim.  This is a triable issue.  It
is important to point out that this is not a summary trial and therefore it is
not the role of the court to examine the evidence closely.  Under the existing
case law it must be plain and obvious that the impugned claims respecting the
collateral agreement and the misrepresentation as to gross sales, gross profits
and operating costs are bound to fail.  Thus, as indicated previously, I am of
the view that only the impugned paragraphs or subparagraphs of the amended
statement of claim that refer to reliance by or misrepresentation to a company
that was not incorporated at the time must be struck out on the basis that
there is no reasonable claim that could be advanced by a company that was not
yet in existence at the time reliance or misrepresentation is pled.

APPLICATION THAT MYA ENTERPRISES POST SECURITY FOR
COSTS

[
39
]

The leading case with respect to this issue is
Kropp v. Swaneset
Bay Golf Course
(1997),
1997 CanLII 4037 (BC CA)
, 29 B.C.L.R. (3d) 252 (C.A.).  Finch J.A. (as he
then was) stated the principles that a court must take into account at para. 17
of that decision:

[17]       In
Keary Development v. Tarmac Construction, [1995] 3 All

E.R.
534, the English Court of Appeal considered s.726(1) of

the
Companies Act 1985, reviewed a number of authorities

applying
that provision or its predecessors, and then set out

the
principles which emerged from those cases.  The principles

are
stated at pp. 539-542, and may be summarized in this way:

1.
The court has a complete discretion whether to order

security, and will act in light of all the relevant

circumstances;

2.
The possibility or probability that the plaintiff company

will be deterred from pursuing its claim is not without

more sufficient reason for not ordering security;

3.
The court must attempt to balance injustices arising from

use of security as an instrument of oppression to stifle a

legitimate claim on the one hand, and use of impecuniosity

as a means of putting unfair pressure on a defendant on

the other;

4.
The court may have regard to the merits of the action, but

should avoid going into detail on the merits unless

success or failure appears obvious;

5.
The court can order any amount of security up to the full

amount claimed, as long as the amount is more than

nominal;

6.
Before the court refuses to order security on the ground

that it would unfairly stifle a valid claim, the court

must be satisfied that, in all the circumstances, it is

probable that the claim would be stifled; and

7.
The lateness of the application for security is a

circumstance which can
properly be taken into account.

[
40
]

In addition to these considerations the court may also consider “the
extent to which the plaintiff’s impecuniosity may be due to the actions of the
of the defendant which form the basis for the plaintiff’s claim” (see Joyce J.
in
Grey v. Power Assist Technologies Inc.
,
2001 BCSC 1208 (CanLII)
, [2001] B.C.J. No. 1722
at para.
19
).

[
41
]

It is clear from the affidavit material referred to by counsel that Mya
does not have the assets to meet an order that it post security for costs.  Further,
it is also clear that the plaintiff Parmar is the sole principal of Mya and he
personally has no assets or means of raising money for Mya to meet such an
order other than the possibility of asking some friend or family member to lend
him money.  Given that there is certainly differing Court of Appeal decisions
with respect to exclusion clauses in franchise agreements, one cannot say that
success is guaranteed and therefore it would be unlikely that Mr. Parmar, on
behalf of Mya, would be able to raise money through borrowing from friends.  As
a result, it is likely that if Mya was ordered to post security for costs, this
action would grind to a halt.

[
42
]

Mr. Parmar, in his affidavit material, has deposed that the only assets
Mya ever had were the franchise and leasehold which was assigned to it, both of
which, of course, it no longer has.  The amended statement of claim is clear in
its assertions and allegations that the loss of those assets was caused by the
defendants’ conduct.

[
43
]

It seems to me that the plaintiffs’ claims are at least arguable and one
cannot say they are obviously bound to fail.

[
44
]

There is certainly nothing to suggest that there is unfair pressure
being placed on the defendants by reason of the impecuniosity of the plaintiffs
in this action.

[
45
]

Utilizing the considerations set out by Finch J.A. in
Kropp v.
Swaneset Bay Golf Course Ltd.
, supra
, and the consideration of
Joyce J. in
Grey v. Power Assist Technologies Inc.
, supra
,
I am of the opinion that it would be unjust, inequitable and unfair to stifle
the claim of the corporate plaintiff who, it appears from the pleadings,
carried on the franchise business from the time it was incorporated.

[
46
]

In the end result, the paragraphs and subparagraphs set out in para. 36
above are struck for the reasons given.  The applicants’ motion for security
for costs is dismissed.  Given that there has been mixed success on the
applicants’ applications, each party will bear their own costs relating to this
hearing.

The
Honourable Mr. Justice Chamberlist
